records.Gloss: curds mixed with salt, chillies, mustard, etc., and some rice flour boiled and seasoned
records.Etymology: 287. Kal. kaḍí, kạí ‘gravy made from meat juices and flour’ is cognate with OIA (Suśr.) khaḍa-, khala- ‘buttermilk boiled with acid vegetables and spices’ (3783). Origin is unclear, but Mayrhofer (EWA) correctly refers to possible Dravidian origin; cf. e.g. Kan. kaḍi ‘curds mixed with salt, chillies, mustard, etc., and some rice flour boiled and seasoned’ (DEDR 1128).

records.Etymology: 147. The following Bng. lemma has already been published (Zoller [1989: 195]), but here follows additional data: Bng. magu adj.,n.m. ‘a little but strong one (boy); a boy’ — Sh.ast. māgī ‘children’ (Nayyar [1986: 45]), cf. PIE *magʰus ‘young man’, but cf. also Sh. maági n.m. ‘darling (no sexual connotation)’ and PN *mag-a ‘young person, child; young’. Note, however, also Ta. maka ‘child, infant, young of animal, son or daughter, young age’ (DEDR 4616), Kan. maga ‘son, male person’, etc. Note: The genuine PIE origin of this ‘lemma’ has been questioned by several scholars, e.g. by Tatyana Mikhailova (2007: 16ff.) who postulates a merger of Nostratic *mVkV and PIE *maghu- ‘fellow, unmarried (p. 17), Ranko Matasović (2009 sub Proto-Celtic *makʷo- ‘son’) and Guus Kroonen (2013) who writes sub Proto-Germanic *magu- ‘boy, relative’ “[a] West European word of obscure origin.”

records.Etymology: 282. Words for cuckoo (or ‘cuckoo’ sounding words designating other birds) are certainly onomatopoeic. But this knockout argument does not mean too much. Within the northwestern and a few other Outer Languages they can be divided into a few groups, in this way disclosing some typological relationships. Note also that some languages have more than one word for ‘cuckoo’. (a) The OIA kokilá- type. The words of this group have not lost the medial -k- just like their Dravidian parallels: Pal. kaˈkūli ‘cuckoo’, Bhad. kākoli ‘cuckoo’ (Kaul [2006 i: 107]), Kaul also gives with- out further West Pahāṛī language specification (2006 i: 32) gaḍkākoli ‘cuckoo of the rivulet’ (but 2006 ii: 395 he says it is from Bhal. meaning ‘pakṣī viśeṣ – type of bird’); in vol. i p. 187 there is the additional alloform Bhal. gaḍ kagholi (with first syllable < OIA *gaḍḍa-¹ ‘hole’ [3981] and note k – gh alternation); there is also the Bng. cuss pũnskōklɔ ‘flatterer, idiot, blockhead’ which cf. with S. kokiḍī ‘stupid as a fowl’; Him. koklā ‘the blackbird’, N. kokʌle ‘cuckoo’ (Z.) and Western Nepal shamanic language kokalsārī ‘cuckoo’ — K. kukilü ‘cuckoo’, Ind. kʌkuìlⁱ ‘cuckoo’ and Bur.ys. káku, kúku ‘cuckoo’ (but note also p. 792 Bur. kápo ‘cuckoo’ and Bur.ys. kíki ‘falcon’) – Ko. koguḷ ‘cuckoo’. Cf. OIA kokilá- ‘cuckoo’ (3483), kukubha- ‘the wild cock Phasianus gallus’ (3210), *kūkkati ‘screams’ (3390), DN: 21 kokk-, kukk- ‘call’ and PMK *kuk, kuuk ‘to call’, but more significant are semantically close Dravidian parallels: Kan. kukil ‘cuckoo’, Tu. kogilè, kojilè ‘cuckoo’, etc. (b) The kuku type which does not have close Dravidian parallels: Kiũṭh. kūkū ‘cuckoo’, Jaun. kūkhū ‘cuckoo’, N. kukku ‘cuckoo’— K. kuku ‘cuckoo’ — Bhaṭ. bã̄kükú ‘type of brown-coloured pheasant’ with first component < vána-¹ ‘forest’ (11258) resembles K. van-kŏkürü ‘a kind of wild bird resembling a barndoor fowl’ but both may rather contain the word for ‘hen’ — Gau. kukʰ ‘type of woodpecker’, Bur.ys. kúku ‘cuckoo’, Kho. káku ‘cuckoo’ and narkˈuku ‘rooster’ (with first syllable < OIA nára- ‘male’ [6970]) — Jaṭ. kak ‘large hill partidge’ — Yid. kakūk ‘cuckoo’. Cf. PIE *kukū ‘cuckoo’. (c) kuku with other extensions: Sutlej Group koklas ‘type of pheasant’ (Malhans [2002: 262]) and Sh.dras. kʌ́kəs ‘pheasant’ (Rajapurohit [2012: 43]) are probably built on the kokilá- basis with vāśuka- element like other ‘pheasant’ words in the northwest (see p. 648 and Aw. kaṭnās ‘a kind of bird [? a jay]’ which may be a case of semantic-morphological amalgamation [on this term see p. 224]). N. kākākul ‘a part. kind of bird’ has a close parallel in Nuristani Kt. kúku kuli ‘cuckoo’ (cf. OIA *kululi- ‘outcry’ [3347]). Kal. kokḍúm ‘cuckoo-like bird’, Kho. kokdˈum ‘coocoo’ (‘cuckoo’) with unclear second component. Rp. kəkcilāṛu ‘a black chicken-like bird’ is a synonym compound: cf. Bng. ċilāṛ ‘cuckoo’ with first syllable < OIA cilli- ‘a kind of bird of prey’ (4829) and Jaun. bhūĩ̄-cīl ‘pheasant’ (with first word < OIA bhú̄mi- ‘earth, ground’ [9557]). More unclear are Psht. kūkūkūtarah ‘a ringdove’ (probably kūkū plus kotar ‘pigeon’), and Mult. and P. kakuhā ‘sandpiper’.

records.Etymology: 302. Garh. karõco ‘fish trap’ < OIA (Pañcat.) kūṭaracana- ‘a laid trap’ which cf. with Kann. khuröṅċ ‘leopard trap’ ; here perhaps also Wg. köv a mesh of branches for catching fish’ without the Indian racana- extension and which is < OIA (R.) kūṭa-⁸ ‘trap for catching deer’ (3397). The CDIAL lemma has reflexes in Pk. and S. to which I add Bng. kuṛiāṇɔ ‘to pursue, chase’ (with -a-, -ā- suffix). According to Mayrhofer, kūṭa-⁸ is probably a borrowing from Dravidian as found e.g. in Kan. gūḍu ‘trap for catching wild animals’. Note also similar sounding OIA matsya-karaṇḍa- ‘a fish-basket, any hamper or receptacle for fish’ built with OIA káraṇḍa-¹ ‘basket’ (2792).
